title: Ganga falls into Shiva's hair
hookLine: a river falls from heaven, Shiva catches it in his hair, and the Rudram bows to rain and to drought
carry: rain or drought, nothing is outside shiva

lines: A KING ASKS FOR A RIVER.
cards: A king named Bhagiratha has one wish: bring the river Ganga down from heaven, so her water can reach the ashes of his ancestors and set them free. After long austerities, he's granted it. But there's a problem.

Ganga is a goddess, and proud, and a river falling from the sky would smash the earth. Only one god can take that weight. So Bhagiratha turns to Shiva, and Shiva stands under the falling sky and opens his matted hair.

teach.b: In the Ramayana's telling, Ganga crashes into his locks and is lost there, wandering in his hair, until Shiva lets her out gently, in streams. The wild water becomes a river that feeds a whole land.
That's why Shiva is pictured with Ganga in his hair. And it's why Ganga water is poured over Shiva's linga: in the month of Shravan, pilgrims carry it on foot, sometimes for days, to pour on him.

teach.h: GOD IN NATURE, GENTLE AND FIERCE.
teach.b: Behind the story is a big Hindu teaching: God isn't only above nature, God is in it, the gentle and the fierce alike. The Rudram said it long before.
A bow to the trees, the green-haired ones: Rudra in the trees, with leaves for hair. A bow to the one in the clouds, and to the one in the lightning.
To the one in the rain, and to the one where no rain falls. To the one in wells, and in the young grass, and in the foam. Rain and no rain: the second half is the surprise.
It's easy to thank God for the rain that feeds the crops. It's harder to bow in a drought.

The Rudram does both, with the same word, because nothing is outside Rudra. Many teachers read Ganga's fall the same way: the force that could flatten the earth and the river that feeds it pass through the same hair.

teach.h: A RIVER CAN BE A GODDESS.
teach.b: That's why, in Hindu eyes, a river can be a goddess and a tree can be holy ground.

how: The Rudram's lines about trees, rain and water are chanted in Vedic Sanskrit as part of the whole Namakam, often during abhishekam in Shiva temples. Ganga water is poured over the linga, and in the month of Shravan pilgrims called kanwariyas carry it on foot to Shiva temples.

o: a god found only on mountaintops, never in rain or drought
a god who catches a falling river in his hair
a god who keeps the river in heaven, away from the earth

games.q: the river and the hymn — tap the pairs.
p: the king who asked for Ganga
where the falling river was gentled

s: Shiva caught Ganga so her fall wouldn't smash the earth
she wandered in his hair until he let her out in streams.
the Rudram bows only to the rain, never to drought
it bows to the one in the rain and to the one where no rain falls.
in Hindu eyes, God sits only above nature, not in it
the Rudram finds Rudra in trees, clouds, wells, grass and foam.

games.q: a long dry summer. you're chanting the Rudram and reach the line about rain. what does the hymn bow to next?
o: the one where no rain falls.
a request to end the drought.
games.why: rain and no rain: the hymn bows to drought as carefully as to rain, because nothing is outside Rudra.

practice: Notice what the weather is doing right now, sun, cloud, rain, wind or still air, and pleasant or not, offer it a small inward bow.
Then, if there's water nearby, pour a little slowly onto a plant or the ground, the way devotees pour Ganga water over the linga, and think of the river Shiva gentled.
If you pray, say namah shivaya as you pour; if you don't, let the pour be your bow.

wordCard.voice: The Rudram. Today's lines: a bow to the green-haired trees, to cloud and lightning, to rain and to drought. And Ganga, caught in Shiva's hair.

orig.note: Sanskrit: green-haired, said of the trees in the Rudram.

carryVoice: Your line: rain or drought, nothing is outside Shiva. Not even the dry ground. Rest well.
